1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# Reclaim local disk by pruning merged git worktrees (and their multi-GB Rust
3	# target/ build caches) plus merged / [gone] local branches. This automates the
4	# recurring "disk maxed by stale worktrees" cleanup: every agent-tool worktree
5	# (.claude/worktrees/*, ~/.t3/worktrees/*) carries its own target/, and nothing
6	# removes them when the branch's PR merges, so they only ever accumulate.
7	#
8	# SAFETY — only work that is provably already in `main` is ever removed:
9	#   * A worktree is removed only if it is CLEAN (no uncommitted tracked changes)
10	#     AND merged: its branch/HEAD is an ancestor of main (plain merge) OR every
11	#     commit's patch is already in main (squash-merge, detected via `git cherry`).
12	#   * A branch is deleted only if it is merged by the same test and is not the
13	#     current branch. In-review branches (unmerged, still alive on origin) and
14	#     anything with commits not represented in main are KEPT and reported.
15	# Nothing that fails the merged test is touched, so no unmerged work is lost.
16	# Even a mistaken worktree removal only drops a regenerable target/ — the branch
17	# ref and its commits survive (recoverable via `git worktree add`).
18	#
19	# Usage:
20	#   scripts/gc.sh          # dry run (default): report what WOULD be removed
21	#   scripts/gc.sh --apply  # actually remove the reported worktrees/branches
22	#
23	# A best-effort `git fetch --prune` runs first so [gone] status and merge checks
24	# are fresh; a network failure is tolerated (falls back to cached refs).
25	set -euo pipefail
26	
27	APPLY=0
28	[ "${1:-}" = "--apply" ] && APPLY=1
29	
30	cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
31	# The real main working tree — NOT the invoking worktree. `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`
32	# returns whichever worktree ran this script, so deriving MAIN_WT from cwd would "protect"
33	# the caller and leave git's actual main checkout eligible for pruning (its branch is `main`,
34	# so is_merged is trivially true). The first `worktree` entry of the porcelain listing is
35	# always the main working tree; parse it exactly as flush_wt parses each entry, so the
36	# equality check below compares like against like.
37	MAIN_WT="$(git worktree list --porcelain | awk '/^worktree / && !found {print substr($0, 10); found=1}')"
38	
39	if [ "$APPLY" -eq 1 ]; then
40	  echo "== gc: APPLY mode — removing merged worktrees and branches =="
41	else
42	  echo "== gc: DRY RUN — nothing will be deleted (pass --apply to act) =="
43	fi
44	
45	# Fresh remote state so [gone]/merge checks are accurate; tolerate offline.
46	if ! git fetch --prune origin >/dev/null 2>&1; then
47	  echo "warn: 'git fetch --prune' failed — using cached remote-tracking refs" >&2
48	fi
49	
50	# Every commit on <ref> already in main? True for a plain-merge ancestor and for
51	# a squash-merge (git cherry prints '+' only for commits whose patch is absent).
52	is_merged() {
53	  local ref="$1" tip
54	  tip="$(git rev-parse --verify "$ref" 2>/dev/null)" || return 1
55	  git merge-base --is-ancestor "$tip" main 2>/dev/null && return 0
56	  ! git cherry main "$tip" 2>/dev/null | grep -q '^+'
57	}
58	
59	# ---- Phase 1: worktrees --------------------------------------------------------
60	# Parse `git worktree list --porcelain` into "path|branch-or-HEAD-sha" records.
61	removed_wt=0
62	wt_path=""; wt_head=""; wt_branch=""
63	flush_wt() {
64	  [ -z "$wt_path" ] && return
65	  # Never touch the main checkout.
66	  if [ "$wt_path" = "$MAIN_WT" ]; then wt_path=""; return; fi
67	  local ref label
68	  if [ -n "$wt_branch" ]; then ref="$wt_branch"; label="[$wt_branch]"; else ref="$wt_head"; label="(detached $wt_head)"; fi
69	  local dirty size
70	  dirty="$(git -C "$wt_path" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null)"
71	  size="$(du -sh "$wt_path" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1)"
72	  if [ -n "$dirty" ]; then
73	    echo "  KEEP  $size  $wt_path $label — uncommitted changes"
74	  elif is_merged "$ref"; then
75	    echo "  PRUNE $size  $wt_path $label — merged"
76	    if [ "$APPLY" -eq 1 ]; then
77	      git worktree remove --force "$wt_path" && removed_wt=$((removed_wt+1))
78	    fi
79	  else
80	    echo "  KEEP  $size  $wt_path $label — NOT merged into main"
81	  fi
82	  wt_path=""
83	}
84	echo "-- worktrees --"
85	while IFS= read -r line; do
86	  case "$line" in
87	    "worktree "*) flush_wt; wt_path="${line#worktree }"; wt_head=""; wt_branch="" ;;
88	    "HEAD "*)     wt_head="${line#HEAD }" ;;
89	    "branch "*)   wt_branch="${line#branch refs/heads/}" ;;
90	    "detached")   wt_branch="" ;;
91	  esac
92	done < <(git worktree list --porcelain)
93	flush_wt
94	[ "$APPLY" -eq 1 ] && git worktree prune
95	
96	# ---- Phase 2: branches (after worktrees gone, so freed branches are deletable) --
97	echo "-- branches --"
98	current="$(git branch --show-current)"
99	# Branches still checked out in a surviving worktree can't be deleted; collect them.
100	checked_out="$(git worktree list --porcelain | sed -n 's/^branch refs\/heads\///p')"
101	removed_br=0
102	while IFS= read -r b; do
103	  [ -z "$b" ] && continue
104	  [ "$b" = "$current" ] && continue
105	  if printf '%s\n' "$checked_out" | grep -qxF "$b"; then
106	    echo "  KEEP  $b — checked out in a worktree"
107	    continue
108	  fi
109	  if is_merged "refs/heads/$b"; then
110	    echo "  DELETE $b — merged"
111	    if [ "$APPLY" -eq 1 ]; then
112	      git branch -D "$b" >/dev/null && removed_br=$((removed_br+1))
113	    fi
114	  else
115	    echo "  KEEP   $b — not merged (in review / unpushed)"
116	  fi
117	done < <(git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads/)
118	
119	echo "== done: removed $removed_wt worktree(s), $removed_br branch(es) =="
120	[ "$APPLY" -eq 0 ] && echo "   (dry run — re-run with 'just gc-apply' to remove the PRUNE/DELETE items)"
121

Full diagnosis complete. Here's what's going on:

## TLDR

`just gc` isn't seeing stale state — it's a blind spot in its squash-merge detection. **Every single worktree/branch it reported as "NOT merged" has in fact merged into main** (I verified all of them against main's history and GitHub's API). The bug: `is_merged` in [gc.sh:52](scripts/gc.sh:52) falls back to `git cherry`, which matches commits by *patch-id* (an exact hash of the diff). That only recognizes a squash merge when the squashed diff is byte-identical to your local commits' diffs. In this repo's workflow — many concurrent PRs touching adjacent files — that's frequently false.

## The concrete evidence

Take `mm-382` as the exemplar. Local branch has one real commit, `3ebb3ad8 "test validator syntax against interop vectors"`. Main has the squash `aca705e9 … (#284)`. Their diffs are identical in 10 of 11 files — but `crates/repo-engine/tests/fixtures/interop/README.md` differs (`14+` on the branch vs `33+/15-` in the squash), because sibling PR #282 ("load real atproto interop vectors") rewrote that same README, and GitHub computed the squash against the newer base. One differing file → different patch-id → `git cherry` says unmerged → gc keeps the 2.4 GB worktree.

The same pattern holds everywhere: mm-387 → merged as #294, mm-368 → #281, mm-307 → #275, mm-360 → #280, mm-392 → #302. The detached worktrees too: `pr-304-continuation` tip is in merged PR #310, `wallet-app-password` in #309, `stoic-northcutt` in #295 (though that one is also *dirty*, which is a legitimate KEEP). GitHub's `commits/<sha>/pulls` endpoint confirms each exact local tip belongs to a merged-into-main PR.

Two things it's **not**: local `main` is not stale (it equals `origin/main` at `4709c5bb`), and `git merge-tree` wouldn't fix it either — I tested, and re-merging the old branch conflicts because main's READMEs kept evolving after the squash.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- `git patch-id` hashes a diff with whitespace/hunk-offset normalization, but it's still *content-exact*. Squash merges survive it only in a quiet repo; any overlap with concurrent PRs, review-round fixups, or conflict resolution during merge breaks equality.
- This is why GitHub itself never uses patch-ids to decide "merged" — it records the PR head SHA at merge time. The `commits/{sha}/pulls` API exposes exactly that association, and it works even for detached HEADs (which have no branch name to query by).
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Recommended fix

Add a third, best-effort tier to `is_merged` in `gc.sh`: when the ancestor and cherry tests both fail, ask GitHub — `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/<tip>/pulls` — and treat the ref as merged iff some associated PR has `merged_at` set and `base.ref` = main. That keeps the "provably in main" safety story (GitHub merged *this exact tip*), works for detached worktrees, and degrades to today's conservative behavior when offline or `gh` is absent.

# Coding Effectively

## Required Sub-Skills

**ALWAYS REQUIRED:**
- `howto-functional-vs-imperative` - Separate pure logic from side effects
- `defense-in-depth` - Validate at every layer data passes through

**CONDITIONAL:** Use these sub-skills when applicable:
- `howto-code-in-typescript` - TypeScript code
- `howto-code-in-rust` - Rust code
- `howto-develop-with-postgres` - PostgreSQL database code
- `programming-in-react` - React frontend code
- `writing-good-tests` - Writing or reviewing tests
- `property-based-testing` - Tests for serialization, validation, normalization, pure functions

## Property-Driven Design

When designing features, think about properties upfront. This surfaces design gaps early.

**Discovery questions:**

| Question | Property Type | Example |
|----------|---------------|---------|
| Does it have an inverse operation? | Roundtrip | `decode(encode(x)) == x` |
| Is applying it twice the same as once? | Idempotence | `f(f(x)) == f(x)` |
| What quantities are preserved? | Invariants | Length, sum, count unchanged |
| Is order of arguments irrelevant? | Commutativity | `f(a, b) == f(b, a)` |
| Can operations be regrouped? | Associativity | `f(f(a,b), c) == f(a, f(b,c))` |
| Is there a neutral element? | Identity | `f(x, 0) == x` |
| Is there a reference implementation? | Oracle | `new(x) == old(x)` |
| Can output be easily verified? | Easy to verify | `is_sorted(sort(x))` |

**Common design questions these reveal:**
- "What about deleted/deactivated entities?"
- "Case-sensitive or not?"
- "Stable sort or not? Tie-breaking rules?"
- "Which algorithm? Configurable?"

Surface these during design, not during debugging.

## Core Engineering Principles

### Correctness Over Convenience

Model the full error space. No shortcuts.

- Handle all edge cases: race conditions, timing issues, partial failures
- Use the type system to encode correctness constraints
- Prefer compile-time guarantees over runtime checks where possible
- When uncertain, explore and iterate rather than assume

**Don't:**
- Simplify error handling to save time
- Ignore edge cases because "they probably won't happen"
- Use `any` or equivalent to bypass type checking

### Error Handling Philosophy

**Two-tier model:**

1. **User-facing errors**: Semantic exit codes, rich diagnostics, actionable messages
2. **Internal errors**: Programming errors that may panic or use internal types

**Error message format:** Lowercase sentence fragments for "failed to {message}".

```
Good: failed to connect to database: connection refused
Bad:  Failed to Connect to Database: Connection Refused

Good: invalid configuration: missing required field 'apiKey'
Bad:  Invalid Configuration: Missing Required Field 'apiKey'
```

Lowercase fragments compose naturally: `"operation failed: " + error.message` reads correctly.

### Pragmatic Incrementalism

- Prefer specific, composable logic over abstract frameworks
- Evolve design incrementally rather than perfect upfront architecture
- Don't build for hypothetical future requirements
- Document design decisions and trade-offs when making non-obvious choices

**The rule of three applies to abstraction:** Don't abstract until you've seen the pattern three times. Three similar lines of code is better than a premature abstraction.

## File Organization

### Descriptive File Names Over Catch-All Files

Name files by what they contain, not by generic categories.

**Don't create:**
- `utils.ts` - Becomes a dumping ground for unrelated functions
- `helpers.ts` - Same problem
- `common.ts` - What isn't common?
- `misc.ts` - Actively unhelpful

**Do create:**
- `string-formatting.ts` - String manipulation utilities
- `date-arithmetic.ts` - Date calculations
- `api-error-handling.ts` - API error utilities
- `user-validation.ts` - User input validation

**Why this matters:**
- Discoverability: Developers find code by scanning file names
- Cohesion: Related code stays together
- Prevents bloat: Hard to add unrelated code to `string-formatting.ts`
- Import clarity: `import { formatDate } from './date-arithmetic'` is self-documenting

**When you're tempted to create utils.ts:** Stop. Ask what the functions have in common. Name the file after that commonality.

### Module Organization

- Keep module boundaries strict with restricted visibility
- Platform-specific code in separate files: `unix.ts`, `windows.ts`, `posix.ts`
- Use conditional compilation or runtime checks for platform branching
- Test helpers in dedicated modules/files, not mixed with production code

## Cross-Platform Principles

### Use OS-Native Logic

Don't emulate Unix on Windows or vice versa. Use each platform's native patterns.

**Bad:** Trying to make Windows paths behave like Unix paths everywhere.

**Good:** Accept platform differences, handle them explicitly.

```typescript
// Platform-specific behavior
if (process.platform === 'win32') {
  // Windows-native approach
} else {
  // POSIX approach
}
```

### Platform-Specific Files

When platform differences are significant, use separate files:

```
process-spawn.ts        // Shared interface and logic
process-spawn-unix.ts   // Unix-specific implementation
process-spawn-windows.ts // Windows-specific implementation
```

### Document Platform Differences

When behavior differs by platform, document it in comments:

```typescript
// On Windows, this returns CRLF line endings.
// On Unix, this returns LF line endings.
// Callers should normalize if consistent output is needed.
function readTextFile(path: string): string { ... }
```

### Test on All Target Platforms

Don't assume Unix behavior works on Windows. Test explicitly:
- CI should run on all supported platforms
- Platform-specific code paths need platform-specific tests
- Document which platforms are supported

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Reality | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| "Just put it in utils for now" | utils.ts becomes 2000 lines of unrelated code | Name files by purpose from the start |
| "Edge cases are rare" | Edge cases cause production incidents | Handle them. Model the full error space. |
| "We might need this abstraction later" | Premature abstraction is harder to remove than add | Wait for the third use case |
| "It works on my Mac" | It may not work on Windows or Linux | Test on target platforms |
| "The type system is too strict" | Strictness catches bugs at compile time | Fix the type error, don't bypass it |

## Red Flags

**Stop and refactor when you see:**

- A `utils.ts` or `helpers.ts` file growing beyond 200 lines
- Error handling that swallows errors or uses generic messages
- Platform-specific code mixed with cross-platform code
- Abstractions created for single use cases
- Type assertions (`as any`) to bypass the type system
- Code that "works on my machine" but isn't tested cross-platform

## Commit Hygiene

Applies to all languages. Commits are the unit of review and bisect; treat them with the same care as the code they contain.

- Each commit is a logical, atomic unit of change.
- Every commit must build and pass all checks (bisect-able history).
- Separate concerns: formatting fixes and refactoring go in separate commits from feature changes.
- Use simple past and present tense in bodies: "Previously X happened. With this commit, Y now happens."
- Commit message bodies use markdown. Do not use backticks in commit titles, but do use them in bodies.

- Why gc went blind in the first place: `git cherry` compares patch-ids, which are content-exact. - The fix leans on the one party that actually knows: GitHub records the head SHA ↔ PR association at merge time, which is precisely the ground truth patch-ids try to approximate.

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line

    }

| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```
